title: Navigating off-target effects in CRISPR-based genome editing for safer gene therapies.
authors: Bhardwaj, Anuradha
abstract: Off-target activity remains a significant challenge in the clinical development of CRISPR-based therapies. As programmable nucleases advance from experimental tools toward approved medicines, the ability to predict, detect, and mitigate unintended genomic editing events has acquired direct translational importance. This review examines the molecular basis of off-target cleavage across three nuclease platforms-zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), and CRISPR-Cas systems-with emphasis on mechanistic and structural factors that govern mismatch tolerance, including PAM sampling, seed region thermodynamics, and chromatin accessibility. In silico prediction methods are surveyed from early alignment-based approaches through feature-engineered machine learning models to more recent deep learning architectures, with critical attention to training data limitations, cross-platform generalisability, and the distinction between exhaustive genomic search tools and predictive scoring models. The experimental detection landscape is reviewed with expanded coverage of established and newer unbiased genome-wide assays, including their biological principles, sensitivity characteristics, and suitability for structural variant detection. Particular attention is given to next-generation editing modalities-base editors, prime editors, and Cas12/Cas13 systems-and to epigenome editing approaches using non-cleaving CRISPR platforms, which avoid double-strand breaks but retain specificity concerns. The review also addresses delivery-related off-target risks, including tissue-level biodistribution and germline exposure, alongside mitigation strategies. It closes by outlining directions for improving standardisation, expanding structural variation surveillance, and extending safety characterisation to the full diversity of editing platforms now approaching clinical use.

title: Decoding gene responsiveness to synthetic chromatin reader-actuators with multi-modal epigenomic profiling.
authors: Kim, Seong Hu; Enwerem-Lackland, Isioma; Williams, Natecia L; Fisher, Rachel; Plaisier, Christopher; Haynes, Karmella A
abstract: Cell identity is regulated by chromatin states that encode gene regulatory memory and shape responses to new inputs. To investigate how chromatin context influences inducibility in differentiated cells, we employed engineered synthetic reader-actuators (SRAs), fusion proteins containing the polycomb chromodomain (PCD) that binds H3K27me3. In MCF7 breast cancer cells, we mapped PCD-fusion occupancy by ChIP-seq and used RNA-seq to identify temporally resolved gene activation patterns. ChIP-seq profiling and machine learning models (MLM) demonstrated that PCD-fusion binding was predicted primarily by the absence of H3K4me3 or H3K9ac enrichment, suggesting selective accessibility at enhancers and chromatin transition zones. Among genes with SRA-enriched enhancers, the SRA-induced subset was distinguished by promoter features including bivalent histone modifications and enrichment of transcription factors NEUROD1 and MTA1. Collectively, our results demonstrate that SRA responsiveness depends on a specific chromatin signature beyond H3K27me3 alone. This study demonstrates the power of SRAs to dissect inducible chromatin features in their native genomic context, and suggests that epigenetically repressed regions in differentiated cells can retain regulatory plasticity.

title: Integrative Structural Modeling of Intrinsically Disordered Regions in a Human HDAC2 Chromatin Remodeling Complex.
authors: Nde, Jules; Kempf, Cassandra G; Zimmermann, Rosalyn C; Cesare, Joseph; Zhang, Ying; Workman, Jerry L; Florens, Laurence; Washburn, Michael P
abstract: Histone deacetylase-containing complexes play central roles in chromatin regulation, yet the structural organization of their intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the previously uncharacterized protein C16orf87, which we renamed MHAP1, as a binding partner of HDAC2 and MIER1. Because all three proteins contain extensive IDRs that remain difficult to study using single structural analysis methods, we employed an integrative structural approach combining cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) with integrative structural modeling to define the architecture of the complex. The resulting integrative structural model reveals that the previously uncharacterized C-terminal IDR of HDAC2 acts as a key interaction hub, engaging both the ELM2 domain of MIER1 and the N- and C-terminal regions of MHAP1. These findings provide the first structural framework for the interactions among HDAC2:MIER1:MHAP1 and demonstrate how intrinsically disordered regions can mediate assembly of a chromatin-associated deacetylase complex. Finally, this research further demonstrates the ability of XL-MS to facilitate integrative structural modeling of protein complexes. Mass spectrometry data may be accessed through ProteomeXchange via PXD082280 and the MassIVE repository MSV000102752.

title: Promoter Engineering in Yeast Cell Factories: Strategies, Applications, and Perspectives.
authors: Bai, Zhenzhen; Jiao, Tian; Darvishi, Farshad; Chu, Haodong; Wang, Zheng; Shi, Shuobo
abstract: Yeasts serve as premier eukaryotic hosts for microbial cell factories, enabling the production of recombinant proteins, biofuels, and high-value natural products. Precise transcriptional control is paramount for balancing complex metabolic pathways and maximizing target product yields. Promoters, as the key regulatory elements governing transcription initiation, have thus become a focal point of metabolic and synthetic biology engineering. This review surveys promoter architecture, function, and engineering in yeast. It outlines promoter structure, from core elements to upstream regulatory sequences, and reviews current and emerging strategies for discovery, optimization, and de novo design, including random mutagenesis, combinatorial assembly, rational design based on transcription factor binding sites, intron-mediated enhancement, cross-species approaches. Importantly, this review highlights the rapidly growing role of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) in promoter engineering, from predictive modeling of promoter strength to in silico generation of synthetic variants. Special emphasis is placed on synthetic promoter engineering to yield tunable and inducible toolkits. The review also highlights applications in yeast cell factories, such as metabolic pathway optimization, dynamic regulation, high-throughput strain screening, and recombinant protein production. By summarizing these recent advances, it serves as a practical resource for researchers aiming to achieve precise metabolic control and improve bioproduction outcomes in yeast.

title: HP1 can act independently of H3K9 methylation to promote heterochromatin focus formation, gene repression, and organogenesis.
authors: Delaney, Colin E; Fol, Lisa; Gruenewald, Stefan B; You, Jia Emil; Ferrario, Eugenio; Moeckel, Martin M; Stelzl, Lukas; Gasser, Susan M; Padeken, Jan; Mango, Susan E
abstract: Histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) segregate genomes into heterochromatin and euchromatin by recruiting readers, such as Heterochromatin Protein 1, which binds methylation of histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me). Here, we report H3K9me-independent functions for the C. elegans HP1 orthologue HPL-2 and the H3K9 methyltransferase MET-2/SETDB1. The two colocalize in H3K9me-containing subnuclear foci independently of the PTM and each other. Their combined loss additively disrupts gene repression and organogenesis. A mutant HPL-2 deficient for H3K9me binding maintains localization to heterochromatin foci, restricts cell-fate decisions, and represses developmental genes, dependent on its multi-zinc-finger ligand, LIN-13. MET-2, catalytically active or not, requires its cofactor LIN-65 to form foci and silence genes in vivo. Molecular dynamics simulations and in vitro assays suggest that cofactor-driven condensate assemblies underlie H3K9me-independent focus formation in vivo, which correlates with gene silencing during organogenesis. This study defines two parallel, PTM-independent pathways through which a writer and reader can repress developmentally regulated genes.

title: Sequence-activity mapping and model-guided engineering of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po sigma(54) promoter.
authors: Xu, Yuxi; Song, Mingxuan; Xing, Wenglong; Han, Jianying; Wu, Jiahao; Cheng, Yi; Liu, Jiayi; Wang, Linfeng; Zeng, Ji; Zhao, Yu; Guo, Jinquan; Cai, Shuting
abstract: Promoters are core cis-regulatory elements that determine gene expression levels and dynamic responses, and their quantitative engineering directly dictates the performance of synthetic biological systems such as whole-cell biosensors. However, the transcriptional output of complex inducible systems, exemplified by sigma(54)-dependent promoters, relies on long-range coordination among distal bacterial enhancer-binding proteins, DNA architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase. The combined effects of multiple regulatory regions on promoter output remain poorly understood, which limits the cross-background transfer of local sequence rules and hinders the accurate prediction and rational design of promoter activity. The phenol-responsive DmpR-Po promoter serves as both a classical model for investigating sigma(54)-dependent regulation and a high-value sensing element for environmental pollutant detection and high-throughput enzyme activity screening. Resolving sequence-activity relationships across its complete regulatory region therefore holds both mechanistic and practical significance. To overcome the barriers to rational engineering of complex promoters, we established a modular design-measure-model-guide-validate framework targeting the full DmpR-Po regulatory region. A library of 17,500 designed promoter sequences was constructed to systematically perturb the upstream activating sequence (UAS), the IHF2 region, combined UAS-IHF2 mutational backgrounds, and downstream regulatory architecture. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting coupled with sequencing yielded a high-quality sequence-activity map covering 11,940 variants. At the regional level, identical UAS and IHF2 haplotypes generally preserved their relative activity rankings across single-region and joint-variant backgrounds, and the main effects estimated independently for UAS and IHF2 could approximately predict the activity of combined variants. At the nucleotide level, however, the effects of individual substitutions were strongly constrained by the overall DNA architecture and full-sequence context. A deep learning model trained on the complete regulatory sequence captured these context-dependent relationships, achieved robust predictive performance on held-out sequences and a separately transformed and processed Batch 2 derived from the same preconstructed plasmid-library pool, and enabled model-guided prioritization of targeted local variants. Single-clone validation further showed that model-guided edits produced variable experimental outcomes, supporting candidate prioritization while indicating that individual engineering predictions require experimental validation. Collectively, this study characterizes the transferability and context-dependent constraints of regional sequence effects and establishes a data-driven framework for quantitative prediction and model-guided engineering of complex sigma(54)-dependent promoters.

title: Disentangling polymer confinement from specific-folding interactions reveals the drivers of Escherichia coli chromosome organization.
authors: Delafrouz, Pourya; Nesterova, Tanya; Harris, Frances E; Farooq, Hammad; Du, Lin; Liu, Jian; Ma, Ao; Xiao, Jie; Liang, Jie
abstract: The three-dimensional organization of the bacterial chromosome is critical for gene regulation. Chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) has enabled genome-wide mapping of chromosomal folding, yet ensemble-averaged contact maps entangle biologically specific-folding interactions (SFIs) with nonspecific polymer compaction and mask single-cell heterogeneity. Here, we developed a polymer-based simulation framework in Escherichia coli to address these limitations. We found that a null model of 300 000 random polymer configurations recapitulated the global chromosomal organization observed in Hi-C data, establishing that most Hi-C signals reflect generic polymer behavior in a confined volume. Contrasting null-model predictions with experimental Hi-C data isolated a small subset of SFIs (<7%) and generated a specific-fold ensemble of 20 000 single-cell conformations that reproduced chromosomal interaction domains and single-cell heterogeneity. SFIs were enriched in the ter region, reduced nucleoid accessibility, colocalized with cryptic prophages, and depleted in positively supercoiled regions. H-NS and MatP emerged as major chromosome-wide and local determinants of SFIs, respectively. Furthermore, high-SFI regions correlated with stress-adaptive genes, whereas low-SFI regions harbored housekeeping genes. Together, our results established that a small number of biologically encoded SFIs superimposed on a polymer background shape the E. coli chromosome and gene expression, providing a quantitative framework for dissecting chromosome architecture and function.

title: Deep dynamical models of single-cell multiomic velocities predict loss-of-function and rescue perturbations in B cells.
authors: Karbalayghareh, Alireza; Pelzer, Benedikt; Chin, Christopher R; Melnick, Ari; Barisic, Darko; Leslie, Christina S
abstract: Here we present DynaVelo, a generative neural ordinary differential equation model that learns the joint dynamics of gene expression and transcription factor (TF) motif activity from single-cell multiome data. DynaVelo learns a functional form of the vector field, such that the model can be perturbed in silico and not only used to draw trajectories. We show that DynaVelo recovers the bifurcating in vivo dynamics of wild-type murine germinal center (GC) B cells and reveals how these dynamics change under heterozygous loss of epigenetic regulators Arid1a and Ctcf. In silico perturbation yields dynamic and cell-state-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that recover known TF-to-gene edges in the wild-type GC GRN and predicts those that are disrupted in mutants. Perturbing Arid1aHet GCs in silico identified Ctcf, Stat3 and Bcl6 as rescue targets for Arid1a loss. In vivo experiments in double-heterozygous mice confirmed rescue of the Arid1aHet dark-zone phenotype in all three cases, and multiome profiling of Arid1aHet;CtcfHet GCs validated the predicted shift toward wild-type dynamics.

title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores.
authors: Sakai, Yuji; Ariyoshi, Mariko; Hirano, Yasuhiro; Mahana, Yutaka; Suzuki, Aussie; Hirota, Toru; Tachikawa, Masashi; Fukagawa, Tatsuo
abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo-electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C-DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

title: Berberine alleviates radiation-induced lung injury by promoting microbiota-derived inosine via the gut-lung axis.
authors: Wang, Shuyuan; Huai, Siyuan; Yuan, Zhen; Ji, Tiannan; Xu, Yinmei; Ren, Yifan; Qian, Niansong; Sun, Shengjie; Li, Jianxiong
abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common complication of radiotherapy. Although berberine (BBR) has been suggested to be associated with reduced RILI incidence, the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we investigated whether the gut microbiota mediates the radioprotective effects of BBR using a C57BL/6 RILI mouse model with 20 Gy thoracic irradiation (n = 6 per group). BBR (100 mg/kg) and inosine (INO, 300 mg/kg) were administered orally in vivo. Antibiotic depletion and fecal microbiota transplantation were performed to assess microbiota dependence. Lung injury was assessed by histology, pulmonary function, and cytokine levels. Gut microbiota was analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and metabolites were profiled using LC-MS/MS. Transcriptomic and epigenomic alterations were assessed by RNA sequencing, ATAC sequencing, and CUT&Tag analysis. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance were used to assess metabolite-protein interactions. We demonstrated that BBR alleviated RILI in a microbiota-dependent manner. BBR increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and metabolite INO levels. Mechanistically, INO was associated with reduced neuron navigator 3 (NAV3) expression, accompanied by decreased chromatin accessibility and increased histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) at the NAV3 locus. Together, these findings reveal a gut microbiota-mediated mechanism underlying BBR-mediated protection against RILI, and suggest microbiota-informed biomarkers for risk stratification.

title: Precision Editing of Cis-Regulatory Elements Drives Crops Quantitative Traits Genetic Improvement: From Functional Dissection to Intelligent Design.
authors: Li, Yulin; Zhang, Xiangyu; Cui, Yongtao; Shang, Guiqi; Wu, Yue; Ma, Yiyuan; Tian, Tian; Liu, Mengru; Sang, Shifei
abstract: Since most agronomic traits are quantitative, ensuring food security under the pressures of global climate change and population growth increasingly relies on the precise and efficient genetic improvement of crop quantitative traits, making it a central focus of breeding research. Traditional breeding and transgenic approaches are often insufficient for modulating complex quantitative traits. In contrast, the advent of gene-editing technologies has opened new avenues for crop genetic improvement. Notably, the editing of cis-regulatory elements allows fine-tuning of gene expression levels and spatiotemporal patterns without altering coding sequences, enabling targeted optimization of quantitative traits such as yield, quality, and stress resistance. This review systematically summarizes the evolution of cis-regulatory element editing technologies, from early random mutagenesis and screening to targeted dissection guided by functional genomics and, more recently, to intelligent design integrating multi-omics and artificial intelligence, highlighting key technologies, representative applications, and inherent limitations at each stage while discussing future research directions in data integration, algorithm development, and tool deployment. We hope this review will provide both theoretical guidance and practical strategies for intelligent crop breeding.

title: Exploring the bistable equilibrium of methylated CpG DNA recognition by the MBD2 protein.
authors: Volkenandt, Senta; Belyaeva, Julia; Li, Torry; Elgeti, Matthias; Metzler, Ralf; Imhof, Petra; Williams, David C Jr; Bagherpoor Helabad, Mahdi
abstract: Methyl-CpG binding domain 2 (MBD2) is a critical epigenetic regulator that selectively binds methylated CpG dinucleotides, key marks controlling gene regulation and chromatin organization. Understanding the interactions and conformational dynamics underlying this high selectivity is essential to elucidate MBD2's regulatory role. Here, using extensive classical MD simulations, we explored the formation of the MBD2-mCpG recognition complex. By initially positioning MBD2 one base pair downstream of its target, we observed its transition to the target site within microseconds. Notably, upon binding, MBD2 adopts two distinct stable conformations: a primary state closely resembling the X-ray crystal structure, and a secondary state of reduced affinity that nevertheless retains comparable selectivity for mCpG. Our results establish S189 as a key macro-switch; loss of its interaction with the methylcytosine backbone shifts the equilibrium toward the secondary state. This is corroborated by MD simulations of the S189A mutant, which preferentially adopts the secondary state-like conformation. Complementary NMR experiments confirm that S189A mutation does not alter mCpG selectivity, while fluorescence polarization measurements reveal a reduced binding affinity, consistent with our MD simulations results. Together, these findings indicate that MBD2 binding to methylated CpG involves a bistable equilibrium, providing new insights into how high affinity and adaptability are balanced in epigenetic recognition. In a broader context, our findings suggest that such alternative bound-state equilibria may represent an inherent feature of specific protein-DNA complexes.

title: Synthesis and Evaluation of Aryloxy-Acetamide Derivatives as CBX2 Inhibitors.
authors: Kawamoto, Yuichiro; Takase, Shohei; Kumar, Ashutosh; Maemoto, Yuki; Zhang, Kam Y J; Ito, Hisanaka; Ito, Akihiro
abstract: The CBX2 protein plays a key role in the methylation of histone lysine residues related to epigenetic silencing. In contrast to other polycomb paralogs, there are few examples of CBX2 modulators, which prompted us to develop small-molecule CBX2 inhibitors by synthetic evolution based on virtual screening hit scaffolds previously reported by our group. We synthesized a series of aryloxy-acetamide derivatives and evaluated their CBX2 inhibitory activities using the NanoBRET assay and the subsequent NanoBiT assay. Through structural modifications, compound 16 was identified as the best CBX2 inhibitor in this series.

title: Differential evolution of neuroinflammatory remodeling programs related to scar formation and regeneration in spinal cord injury: A cross-species multi-omics analysis.
authors: Tang, Hao; Cheng, Fei; Xu, Juan; Liao, Huiming; Lu, Shunfei; Fu, Xin; Fang, Sheng
abstract: Spinal cord injury in mammals often transitions from an acute inflammatory response to persistent neuroinflammatory and scar-associated remodeling, whereas zebrafish attenuate injury-induced inflammatory programs during regenerative repair. The molecular programs underlying these divergent outcomes remain incompletely understood. In this study, we integrated phase-aligned mouse and zebrafish spinal cord injury datasets using single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, pathway and regulon analyses, expression-based ligand-receptor co-expression analysis, machine-learning validation, chromatin-accessibility profiling, in silico perturbation modeling, and mouse tissue validation. Cross-species analysis revealed a conserved injury-responsive program associated with secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) and CD44, but with distinct temporal trajectories between species. In mouse spinal cord injury, Spp1 and Cd44 expression remained elevated from acute injury through scar-associated stages and was enriched within lesion-associated myeloid and glial-immune microenvironments. Persistent SPP1-CD44-associated expression was accompanied by inflammatory signaling, reactive gliosis, fibrotic remodeling, and sustained immune-niche remodeling. In zebrafish, spp1 and cd44a were similarly induced during the early injury response but declined during regenerative recovery, consistent with attenuation and reorganization of inflammatory programs rather than absence of early injury activation. Machine-learning analyses supported the cross-dataset reproducibility of SPP1-CD44-related injury-state features across two mouse spinal cord injury datasets. Regulon, perturbation-associated, and chromatin-accessibility analyses further positioned Spp1 within an injury-responsive regulatory context associated with signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 and SMARCA4 (SWI/SNF related, matrix associated, actin dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily a, member 4) states and identified perturbation-sensitive accessibility changes at the Spp1 promoter. Mouse spinal cord injury tissue validation confirmed increased SPP1 and CD44 protein expression after injury and localized enhanced SPP1 signal to ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1-positive lesion-associated myeloid regions. Together, these findings suggest that mammalian spinal cord injury scarring is associated with persistence of a conserved SPP1-CD44-associated neuroinflammatory remodeling program, whereas attenuation of the corresponding program accompanies regenerative spinal cord repair in zebrafish. This cross-species framework provides molecular insights and candidate regulatory programs for future studies aimed at promoting inflammatory resolution and neural repair after spinal cord injury.

title: Predicting cell-state-specific gene regulation from DNA across species
authors: Liu H; Mao S; Gallent T; Chen Y; Yan Z; Vogel I; Traunmuller L; Zhang R; Buenrostro JD; Zhou J; Greenberg ME
abstract: DNA encodes the cell's phenotype, but the same DNA sequence is interpreted differently in every cell type, developmental stage, and activity state. Existing deep-learning models solve only half of this puzzle: sequence-to-function models read DNA but treat cell state as a fixed label, while single-cell foundation models represent cell state but not sequence. We developed Bolero, a sequence-to-function model whose parameters condition on atlas-scale cell-state embeddings and additional biological variables to predict cell-state-specific chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance from DNA. Trained on 10.7 million cells from 33 datasets across six mammals, Bolero matched or exceeded specialised models and resolved regulatory differences between closely related cell states, including cortical regional and developmental gradients. Extrapolating cell-state embeddings extended Bolero's predictions to cell states that are absent from training. Cell-state conditioning facilitated tracing of the effects of non-coding variants to the cell types in which they act. Using an AP-1 activity score as a further continuous conditioning axis, Bolero predicted activity-regulated chromatin changes without requiring actual stimulation data. Across human cell types, we reconstructed the cooperative grammar of motif identity and spacing underlying predicted AP-1 responses. Bolero further predicted cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and AP-1 responses in species excluded from training, extending comparative genomics from sequence conservation to predicted functional conservation. Across 84 mammals, we found that predicted AP-1 responses were less conserved than chromatin accessibility at cis-regulatory elements, driven by the human-specific sequence variants on AP-1 and cooperating motifs. By combining reference genomes with reference cell atlases, Bolero allowed genome sequences, either native or mutated, to be queried across cell states, perturbations, and different species for their chromatin and expression signatures.

title: Reconstructing human gene regulatory evolution using deep learning
authors: Yamada T; Yuan X; Zeberg H; Soltys V; Lana Alberro M; Sarropoulos I; Paabo S; Kaessmann H
abstract: Understanding the genetic changes that drove the evolution of human-specific traits is a central goal in biology. Changes in gene expression are thought to be a major source of phenotypic innovations, but identifying the underlying changes in cis-regulatory elements (CREs) along the human lineage has been difficult: functional data from great apes are scarce and unobtainable for extinct hominins, and pinpointing causal substitutions requires knowing which sequences determine CRE activity. Here, we used AlphaGenome, a sequence-to-function deep-learning model, to predict the cis-regulatory effects of ~17 million single-nucleotide substitutions specific to the human lineage and traced their consequences for gene expression evolution across 305 tissues and cell types. The 71,345 predicted cis-regulatory gains lie mostly outside human accelerated regions and arose either through creation of new CREs or, more often, through co-option of CREs ancestrally accessible in other tissues. They are also enriched for distal enhancers and for target gene functions characteristic of the corresponding tissues, suggesting that they contributed to the evolution of tissue-specific biology in humans. Genes linked to more gains were more likely to be upregulated in humans, and in silico reversion to ancestral alleles traced such upregulations to individual substitutions creating transcription factor binding motifs. Comparison with Neandertal and Denisovan genomes revealed that nearly all gains now fixed in humans predate the split from archaic hominins, yet a few modern-human-specific gains contribute substantially to gene upregulation. Our study provides a genome-wide, tissue-resolved map of cis-regulatory changes and their contribution to gene expression evolution along the human lineage.

title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
authors: Lai J; Xin B; Wang Z; Yu A; Chen Z; Guo Y; Zhang M; Hu B; Ye C; Chen J; Liu Q; Zhao H; Song W; Dong N; Yang F; Yang Q; Zhao H
abstract: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.

title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
authors: Sihan Liu; Hongbo Zhao; Andrej Košmrlj
abstract: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

title: An autoencoder outperforms two transformers on prediction of gene expression from chromatin accessibility
authors: Jesse G. Meyer
abstract: Models that predict RNA abundance from chromatin accessibility are rarely compared under the same features, targets and metrics. We built one benchmark on 126,604 paired single-nucleus profiles from 19 human studies with a shared vocabulary of 50,000 peaks and 3,185 genes, ten 5x2 cross-validation folds and one scoring target, and compared seven implemented pipelines and two reference predictors across 70 trained runs; each pipeline keeps its own input normalisation and native training target. The scButterfly-B pipeline, built on dual variational autoencoders, outperformed every transformer pipeline, including an autoregressive Perceiver model (Omic Translator) and a support-free reformulation of Cisformer, on per-gene and within-cell Spearman correlation in all sixty paired fold comparisons, with 3.8 times shorter training. Transformer pipelines come within 0.02-0.04 on within-cell profile shape but lag by 0.10-0.24 on per-gene correlation. On two withheld cell types per-gene correlation is low; controls show the podocyte values are typical of within-type correlation for seen cell types of the same size, whereas Paneth values match a cell-agnostic shuffle for every Omic Translator arm. Within the transformer family, prespecified ablations show the Perceiver encoder was worth +0.0439 in within-donor per-gene correlation over full self-attention, a chromosome-aware genomic attention prior reduced it by 0.0096 (exact donor-level sign-flip test, Holm-adjusted p = 1.2e-4), and decoder output order had no detectable effect. A training-mean profile reaches 0.314 within-cell correlation with no input and a constant at the true expressed-gene positions reaches 0.996 per-gene correlation, so oracle-support protocols are reported only as diagnostics. Code, results and an audited release are provided.

title: Functional fine-mapping of the 9p21.3 cardiovascular disease locus implicates the lncRNA MIR31HG as an effector transcript in endothelial cells
authors: Zhigulev A; Poujade F; Gryzunov N; Buyan A; Li H; Bergman O; Liu M; Pradhananga S; Franco-Cereceda A; Swoboda P; Kulakovskiy IV; Eriksson P; Sahlén P; Björck HM
abstract:
BACKGROUND

The chromosome 9p21.3 locus is among the strongest genetic risk loci for cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. Previous vascular disease studies focused predominantly on the role of this locus in smooth muscle cell (SMC) dysfunction, whereas its potential role in endothelial cells (ECs) remains less well characterized. Here, we sought to identify candidate regulatory variants at 9p21.3, their distal target genes, and effector transcripts that contribute to CVD-related phenotypes in ECs.

METHODS

Promoter capture Hi-C was used to map chromatin interactions at 9p21.3 in primary human ascending aortic SMCs (n=6), supplementing the previously obtained ECs (n=16) dataset. To support the regulatory relevance of these interactions, expression quantitative trait locus analysis was performed in 136 vascular biopsies. Variant effects were prioritized in silico using AlphaGenome. The regulatory activity of the prioritized region was validated using CRISPR activation.

RESULTS

Chromatin interaction mapping identified a complex regulatory architecture at the 9p21.3 locus involving 19 putative regulatory elements and 15 genes across ECs and SMCs. MIR31HG showed the most recurrent distal promoter connectivity with the 9p21.3 region. Consistent with the chromatin interaction map, expression of MIR31HG transcripts was associated with genetic variation at the 9p21.3 locus. In ECs, the lncRNA MIR31HG, but not miR-31, was responsive to hemodynamic flow. Depletion of MIR31HG in ECs was associated with endothelial activation. Epigenetic tracks and deep learning predictions highlighted an active enhancer element at 9p21.3, which was subsequently validated by CRISPR activation and increased MIR31HG expression, confirming its capacity to regulate MIR31HG over a large genomic distance of approximately 538 kb.

CONCLUSIONS

Altogether, these data implicate lncRNA MIR31HG as a likely effector of the 9p21.3 CVD locus, linking the cis-regulatory element and heritable genetic variation in the respective region to endothelial activation through long-range enhancer regulation.

Clinical Perspective

What Is New? Promoter capture Hi-C in primary human vascular cells identified recurrent long-range interactions between the 9p21.3 cardiovascular disease locus and the MIR31HG promoter, extending the regulatory landscape beyond the nearest genes. Expression of MIR31HG transcripts was associated with 9p21.3 genetic variation in vascular tissue; the lncRNA MIR31HG was responsive to hemodynamic flow in endothelial cells and influenced the endothelial activation transcriptional programs upon depletion. Integrated sequence-based, epigenomic, genetic, and CRISPR activation analyses nominated the 9p21.3 enhancer as a regulator of MIR31HG in endothelial cells. What Are the Clinical Implications? The findings suggest that the cardiovascular disease associations of 9p21.3 may involve stronger than previously anticipated endothelial regulatory mechanisms in addition to characterized effects in other vascular cell types. lncRNA MIR31HG provides a molecular link between noncoding genetic variation at 9p21.3 and endothelial cell-state regulation relevant to vascular disease.
